claims.text: At stage-0, orders records its customer only as the number customer_id; the seed has 12 orders and 5 customers; order 3 has customer_id 2, and customer 2 is Nguyễn Bảo Châu.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang@stage-0: db/schema.sql l.18-24 (orders); db/seed.sql l.16-35

claims.text: A join is written inside the FROM clause: T1 [INNER] JOIN T2 ON condition, or T1 LEFT [OUTER] JOIN T2 ON condition; the ON condition is a boolean expression, tested for each pair of rows.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs §7.2.1.1 Joined Tables (Qualified joins)

claims.text: For each row of the left table, the joined table has one row per right-table row that passes ON; a joined row holds the left table's columns, then the right table's. The SELECT list then chooses which columns the result shows, and in what order.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs §7.2.1.1 Joined Tables (INNER JOIN; column order of a joined table)

claims.text: LEFT JOIN: an inner join is performed first; then for each row of T1 that satisfies the condition with no row of T2, a row is added with nulls in T2's columns. The result always has at least one row per T1 row.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs §7.2.1.1 Joined Tables (LEFT OUTER JOIN)

claims.text: A cross join (Cartesian product) of tables with N and M rows has N*M rows, every row of one paired with every row of the other. FROM T1, T2 (comma, no WHERE linking them) is equivalent to T1 CROSS JOIN T2, so FROM orders, customers returns 60 rows.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs §7.2.1.1 Joined Tables (Cross join: N * M rows; equivalence with FROM T1, T2)

claims.text: The join definitions say which rows result, not how PostgreSQL computes them; the planner can choose among several join methods and the result is the same.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs §7.2.1.1; §50.5 Planner/Optimizer (nested loop, merge join, hash join)

claims.text: Every JOIN ... ON in db/queries/*.sql at stage-0 compares a foreign key with the primary key it references (orders.customer_id = customers.id, order_items.order_id = orders.id, payments.order_id = orders.id).
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang@stage-0: db/queries/join-orders-customers.sql, left-join-customers-without-orders.sql, revenue-by-customer.sql; db/schema.sql

claims.text: A join condition usually compares a foreign key with the primary key it references, when the schema records the link between two tables as a foreign key; other conditions are allowed.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs §5.5.5 Foreign Keys; §7.2.1.1 (any boolean ON condition)

claims.text: orders.customer_id is NOT NULL and REFERENCES customers (id), so each order has exactly one customer. Seed: customers 1-4 have three orders each (1: 1, 2, 10; 2: 3, 4, 11; 3: 5, 6, 7; 4: 8, 9, 12); customer 5 has none.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang@stage-0: db/schema.sql l.18-24; db/seed.sql l.23-35

claims.text: FROM orders AS o gives the table the alias o, and the table is then referred to as o (o.id). expr AS name in the SELECT list names the output column. Prefixing a column with its table's alias says which table's column it is.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs §7.2.1.2 Table and Column Aliases; §7.3.2 Column Labels; §4.2.1 Column References

claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs §9.21 Aggregate Functions (count(*))

claims.text: psql prints a null value as nothing (an empty cell) by default.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs, psql reference, \pset null (default prints nothing)

claims.text: WHERE is applied to the rows FROM produces, joins included, so it sees the null-filled rows a LEFT JOIN adds. IS NULL is true exactly for a null value, unlike = NULL, which yields null for every row, so WHERE o.id = NULL keeps no row.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs, SQL Commands: SELECT, Description (FROM, then WHERE); §9.2 Comparison Functions and Operators (IS NULL)

claims.text: A primary key's values must be unique and not null, so orders.id is never null in a stored row.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs §5.5.4 Primary Keys; examples/don-hang@stage-0 db/schema.sql l.19

claims.text: With ON c.id = c.id in place of line 10's condition (c.id is a non-null primary key), the condition holds for every pair: 12 orders x 5 customers = 60 rows, returned without an error; each order appears five times.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs §7.2.1.1 (inner join semantics); examples/don-hang@stage-0 db/schema.sql, db/seed.sql

claims.text: For the INNER and OUTER join types a join condition must be specified, exactly one of ON, USING or NATURAL; INNER JOIN or LEFT JOIN with none is rejected with an error, returning no rows. CROSS JOIN takes no condition.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs, SQL Commands: SELECT, FROM Clause (join_type, join_condition)

claims.text: When you write or change a join, compare the row count with the number you expect, because a wrong condition changes the count while each row still looks normal.
Without ORDER BY, rows are returned in an unspecified order.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs §7.5 Sorting Rows

claims.text: With the same ON condition, LEFT JOIN returns the INNER JOIN rows plus one null-filled row per unmatched left row, so the two return the same rows when every left row has a match. Seed: customers INNER JOIN orders gives 12 rows without customer 5; LEFT JOIN gives 13.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs §7.2.1.1 Joined Tables (LEFT OUTER JOIN defined as inner join plus added rows); examples/don-hang@stage-0 db/seed.sql

claims.text: Grouping the joined rows by the order's id (GROUP BY) turns them back into one row per order.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs §7.2.3 The GROUP BY and HAVING Clauses
